title: Emerging Legal Frameworks
answer: Machine authorship, autonomous entities, multi-agent liability, deepfake evidence and the right to an explanation.

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: This page examines the legal point at which output produced with artificial intelligence counts as authored by a human for copyright, patent, or related rights.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries covers legal questions about whether and how software systems that act with little or no human intervention can hold duties, own assets, or be held responsible.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: This page covers legal responsibility when two or more AI agents act together or against each other without a human directing each step.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes and evidentiary standards concern how synthetic media, especially manipulated video, audio, and images, are treated when offered as proof in court.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation concerns whether a person affected by an automated decision can obtain a meaningful account of how that decision was made.

sections.body: Emerging legal frameworks cover the rules that courts and legislatures are building for systems that create, decide, and act. Machine authorship asks whether a text or image produced by a model can have an author under copyright law. Autonomous entities raise the question of whether software can hold property, sign contracts, or owe duties like a trustee. Multi-agent liability deals with harm when two or more AI systems trade, bid, or coordinate without a human in the loop. Deepfake evidence concerns audio and video that may be fabricated and how courts decide what is real. The right to an explanation covers whether a person affected by an automated decision can demand a reason for it.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is early and fragmented. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows how much is still being argued rather than settled. No court has produced a stable rule for machine authorship, and different jurisdictions treat autonomous entities differently. Multi-agent liability has almost no case law because the technology is new and harms are hard to trace to a single actor. Deepfake evidence rules vary by state and often rely on expert testimony that can be challenged. The right to an explanation exists in some privacy laws but is limited to certain decisions and rarely gives a full technical account.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the creator to the system to the harm to the evidence to the remedy. A reader asking whether a model can own its output would begin with The Threshold of Machine Authorship. From there, Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries explains what happens when software is given legal powers like a person or a trustee. Liability When Agents Interact then covers the harder problem of assigning fault when two or more systems cause damage together. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards shifts to the courtroom and how judges handle fabricated media. The Right to an Explanation closes the loop by asking what a person can demand after an automated decision affects them.
